id: No King, No King of Kings

prompts.L1:

has ever lit up our hearts like this. No king. See Bhutto in Karachi, 1972. His path strewn with rose petals, sprinkled with attar, leads him, not to the sea with its crashing surf and screaming gulls but into the alleys and passageways of a slum. Ferdowsi in Shahnamah tags it for the interim as “the place of worship before any others existed. . . ” No King, no King of Kings, had ever toured a slum before. outputs.L2:
No ruler had ever moved us so deeply. None. Think of Bhutto in Karachi in 1972. A route covered with rose petals and scented with attar takes him—not toward the ocean, with its pounding waves and shrieking gulls—but through the narrow lanes and corridors of a shantytown. In the *Shahnamah*, Ferdowsi provisionally names such a place “the place of worship before any others existed . . .” Never before had a king, not even a King of Kings, walked through a slum.

That moment unlocked, as if by force, the heavily sealed chamber of compassion within us. The crowds gather, hoping only to see Bhutto, but what appears before them is a doubled image: Alexander the Great in a crimson robe, his left hand on his sword, as though lifted from a *Shahnamah* illustration, looking on while our own pilgrim, the unaware Bhutto, “reaches for the door handle of the Ka'ba.” Bhutto’s aides and the PTV news team try to hold back. The crowd, thrown off balance and filled with the force of this vision, presses Bhutto toward the shack of a woman whom poverty has nearly driven mad. Radiant, with tears in his eyes, Bhutto takes the woman into his arms as she falls against him. No monarch, no King of Kings, had ever illuminated our hearts in such a way. No king.
outputs.L3:
Bhutto’s visit to a Karachi slum in 1972 is presented as an extraordinary and unprecedented act of compassion by a political leader. The scene emphasizes that he did something no ruler had done before: he entered a neighborhood marked by extreme poverty, neglect, and suffering. His presence among the poor is portrayed not merely as a political gesture, but as a deeply emotional moment that seemed to break the traditional distance between rulers and the people.

The passage contrasts Bhutto with kings, conquerors, and legendary rulers of the past. It suggests that while many great rulers had commanded armies, built empires, or inspired fear and admiration, none had shown the humility to step into such a deprived community. By entering the slum, Bhutto is represented as surpassing those earlier figures in moral significance. His act is framed as a new kind of greatness, based not on power or conquest, but on compassion and closeness to the suffering masses.

For the crowd, Bhutto’s arrival becomes almost visionary. The people do not experience him simply as an ordinary politician visiting their area; instead, his presence is described in elevated, almost mythical terms. Images associated with Alexander the Great and sacred pilgrimage blend into the scene, giving Bhutto’s visit a heroic and spiritual quality. The crowd’s reaction suggests that they see him as a figure of destiny, someone whose appearance among them transforms their misery into a moment of collective hope and devotion.

The emotional climax of the scene occurs when Bhutto embraces a poverty-stricken woman. This gesture becomes the most powerful symbol of the visit. In embracing her, Bhutto appears to acknowledge the suffering of the poorest and most forgotten members of society. The moment is portrayed as intensely moving because it collapses the distance between leader and subject, privilege and deprivation, authority and helplessness. The woman’s poverty makes the embrace even more meaningful, turning it into an image of mercy, recognition, and human solidarity.

Overall, the passage presents Bhutto as a leader who awakened deep feelings of love, mercy, and devotion in the hearts of the people. His visit is described not simply as a political event, but as a moment of emotional and symbolic transformation. Through his compassion, Bhutto is shown as inspiring the poor to feel seen, valued, and spiritually uplifted. The text therefore constructs him as a figure of exceptional moral power, one whose greatness lies in his ability to reach the hearts of ordinary people.
outputs.L4:

The scene does not depict him simply as a politician arriving among the poor; instead, it elevates him into a figure of sacred and royal significance. His presence is compared to that of a saint, a savior, or a king, suggesting that his visit carries emotional and symbolic weight far beyond an ordinary public appearance. Through this imagery, the text emphasizes the extraordinary nature of his decision to enter the world of the dispossessed and to stand physically among people who had long been ignored by those in power.

The most powerful moment in the account occurs when Bhutto encounters an impoverished and suffering woman. Rather than keeping the formal distance usually associated with rulers and political leaders, he embraces her. This gesture becomes the emotional center of the scene. It transforms the visit into an act of recognition: the misery of the poor is not merely observed but acknowledged with tenderness and human warmth. The woman’s suffering comes to represent the suffering of the wider population, and Bhutto’s response suggests that he is capable of feeling and sharing the pain of ordinary people.

As a result, the public is deeply moved. The embrace awakens compassion in those who witness it and becomes a symbol of a new kind of leadership. Bhutto is portrayed as someone who surpasses the limits of traditional kingship, not by displaying wealth, power, or grandeur, but by showing empathy. The text suggests that true greatness lies in a leader’s ability to inspire hope among the most vulnerable. In this portrayal, Bhutto’s visit becomes more than a political event: it becomes a moment of emotional renewal, in which the poor are seen, their suffering is dignified, and the possibility of a more compassionate future is briefly made visible.

Karachi is a city where history, politics, and daily life meet in a powerful way. When people see Karachi, they often notice its busy streets, seaside views, markets, and the energy of millions of residents. It is not only Pakistan’s largest city but also an important center of culture, trade, and political activity.

The name Bhutto is closely connected with Pakistan’s political history. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and later Benazir Bhutto played major roles in shaping national politics, and their influence has been strongly felt in Sindh, including Karachi. For many people, the Bhutto family represents both hope and controversy, democracy and struggle.

To see Karachi through the lens of the Bhutto legacy is to understand a city shaped by ambition, diversity, conflict, and resilience. Karachi continues to grow and change, carrying with it the memories of Pakistan’s past and the possibilities of its future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, postcolonial prose passage about Zulfikar Ali Bhutto visiting a Karachi slum in 1972, blending political mythmaking with imagery from Ferdowsi’s Shahnamah and Alexander the Great.
counterfactuals.output:
In the year after the sundering, when the map was still wet with ink and grief, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto came down to the lanes of Karachi where the city had hidden its broken teeth.

It was 1972, and the sea wind carried salt, diesel, and the sour breath of open drains. Tin roofs trembled in the afternoon heat. Children with dust-bright faces ran beside the motorcade as though pursuing a comet fallen from the firmament. Women watched from doorways curtained with saris faded by sun and smoke. Men in sweat-darkened shirts gathered around him with the wary hope of those who had heard too many promises turn to ash.

Bhutto stepped out in his tailored suit, a prince among patched awnings, and the slum leaned toward him.

In later tellings, they would say he did not merely walk there; he entered like a figure from the *Shahnamah*, crossing not a gutter but the Oxus, not a quarter of Karachi but the battlefield between humiliation and destiny. Some would name him Rustam, lifting the mace of the people against the white demons of hunger. Others, less forgiving, would see in him the gleam of Iskandar’s mirror: Alexander’s hunger for the world, polished into charm, reflecting back to every crowd the face it longed to see.

He raised his hand, and for a moment the alley became an assembly hall, the cracked earth a throne room, the barefoot poor his witnesses and his crown. Pakistan, wounded and newly diminished, hovered behind him like a defeated kingdom in Ferdowsi’s lament—its kings dead, its warriors scattered, its mothers beating their breasts at the gates of history. Yet here, amid kerosene smoke and flies, Bhutto spoke as if the epic had not ended. He promised bread, cloth, shelter: three small words, but in that place they sounded like treasures seized from the vaults of Kay Kavus, like water discovered in the desert by an army ready to mutiny.

The people listened. They had known conquerors before: men who arrived with ledgers, rifles, censuses, borders, doctrines, English syllables hardened into law. They had been named, counted, displaced, employed, dismissed. Empires had passed over them like dust storms. Now this son of landlords and foreign schools stood before them speaking the language of dispossession, turning poverty into a banner, turning the slum into a stage on which the nation might be reborn.

A boy climbed a broken wall to see him better. In his imagination Bhutto’s dark hair became a helmet, his voice a bronze trumpet, his outstretched arm the sign by which armies move. The boy did not know the names of Persepolis or Macedon, did not know how Alexander rode east with philosophers and fire, how he shattered old thrones and borrowed their splendor. But he understood conquest. He had seen it in the price of flour, in the policeman’s baton, in the landlord’s thumbprint, in the factory gate that opened and closed like fate.

Bhutto smiled, and the crowd surged.

There was tenderness in the moment, and theatre too. Postcolonial history often arrives costumed twice: first as injury, then as performance. A nation stripped by empire must dress itself in legend. So the leader becomes warrior, lover, martyr, shah; the people become chorus; the slum becomes the plain of battle. Above the corrugated roofs, the kites circled like the simurgh searching for a child abandoned on the mountain.

He bent to touch an old man’s shoulder. Cameras clicked. Somewhere a party worker shouted slogans until his throat cracked. Someone wept. Someone laughed. Someone, already experienced in the arithmetic of power, wondered how long it would take for the drains to be covered, the school to be built, the ration card to arrive.

But that afternoon did not belong to arithmetic. It belonged to the intoxication of being seen.

For a little while, in that Karachi basti, the defeated felt summoned back into the epic. The refugee, the laborer, the widow, the hawker, the child with no shoes: each stood in the dust of empire’s aftermath and heard himself addressed as citizen. Bhutto gave them not yet justice, not yet bread, but a grander hunger—the belief that their suffering could be spoken aloud in the language of kings.

And he, moving through the alleys with the sea behind him and the ruin of the old Pakistan before him, seemed both Rustam and Iskandar: champion and conqueror, redeemer and mirror, a man fashioning myth from the raw material of need. The slum received him as the earth receives monsoon clouds—knowing that clouds may pass without rain, yet lifting its face all the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, literary paragraph in the style of a historical novel where Bhutto’s tour of a poor neighborhood becomes a quasi-sacred event, with crowds, PTV cameras, rose petals, attar, and repeated “No king” refrain.
counterfactuals.output: By noon the lanes had ceased to be lanes and become a single breathing body, a poor quarter transfigured by rumor into procession, its open drains veiled with rose petals, its cracked walls hung with bedsheets and party colors, its children scrubbed and shining as if for Eid; and when Bhutto’s car nosed slowly through the press of bodies, the whole mohalla leaned toward him as toward a relic borne from a shrine. PTV cameras, solemn on their tripods, blinked their official eyes while men on rooftops flung fistfuls of petals that fell upon the bonnet, the policemen, the uplifted hands, the dust itself, until even poverty seemed briefly perfumed; women behind lattices tipped tiny bottles of attar onto cotton and passed the scent down through the crowd like a blessing. “No king,” someone cried, and the cry multiplied—“No king, no king”—not quite slogan, not quite prayer, rising from the barefoot boys, the mill workers, the widows in faded dupattas, from those who had never owned anything but a ration card and a memory of hunger. He stood in the open car, pale suit spattered red with roses, smiling with that grave theatrical tenderness which made strangers believe they had been seen, and for a moment the neighborhood, filmed for the nation and fragrant as a tomb on a saint’s day, imagined itself not ruled but chosen. “No king,” the crowd thundered again, though the cameras drank him in like coronation lamps; “No king,” they swore, even as petals crowned his hair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental vignette that mythologizes a Pakistani leader entering a slum, comparing him to kings and epic heroes while showing how the poor crowd experiences the moment as miraculous.
counterfactuals.output:
When the Leader entered the basti, the lane narrowed as if history itself had bent down to look.

He did not arrive like a man, though men flanked him—men with polished shoes darkened by open drains, men lifting their trouser hems from the black water, men whispering into phones as if reporting to distant planets. He arrived like a rumor from the age of kings: a figure stepping out of heat-shimmer and siren, his white shalwar kameez burning softly in the dust, the sun caught on his brow like a coin minted by some vanished empire.

The children saw him first.

They had been flying a kite made from a torn election poster, its paper face patched with flour paste and string. It dipped above the corrugated roofs, above the blue plastic sheets weighted with bricks, above the television antennas bent like exhausted spears. Then the motorcade stopped where no motorcade had ever stopped before, and the kite collapsed into the arms of a boy who forgot to be afraid.

“Badshah,” someone murmured.

Not because he wore a crown. He wore none. But the poor have old eyes. They know the shapes power takes when it enters their alleys: the tax collector’s ledger, the policeman’s stick, the landlord’s thumb on a document, the candidate’s smile before the vanishing. Yet this was different, or seemed different in that molten instant. The Leader’s hand lifted—not grandly, not from a balcony, but close enough that the women behind the doorways could see the veins under his skin.

And so the basti began to rearrange him into legend.

He became Sikandar crossing not the Indus but the gutter between two broken paving stones. He became Rustam lowering his horse’s head before a clay stove. He became a Mughal emperor dismounting at the threshold of hunger, a saint-king from a grandmother’s qissa, the one who comes disguised to weigh the city’s sorrow in his palm.

The air changed.

A mechanic wiped grease from his hands and stood straighter than he had in years. A widow, whose roof leaked during every monsoon, pressed her fingers to her lips and then to her forehead as though witnessing a relic. An old fruit seller, nearly blind, began to weep without understanding why; perhaps because the Leader’s shadow had fallen across his wooden cart, and for one second the flies rose away from the guavas like defeated demons.

No miracle occurred, and yet everything became miraculous.

The open sewer remained open. The electric wires still sagged low enough to kill a careless child. The pump at the corner still coughed rust-colored water. But the people, packed shoulder to shoulder, felt reality loosen around them. A woman lifted her sick daughter above the crowd, not so he could cure her—no one said cure—but so his gaze might touch the child’s face. A boy with no shoes ran beside him, laughing, convinced that if he could match the Leader’s stride for three steps he would inherit some invisible strength.

The Leader paused before a wall scribbled with old slogans and new stains. He listened to a man speak of rent, to a mother speak of fever, to a teenager speak of work that never came. Cameras hovered. Microphones leaned forward like hungry birds. But in the crush of bodies, beyond the machinery of spectacle, another drama unfolded: the poor saw themselves reflected in the attention of the powerful and mistook, for a breath, recognition for deliverance.

In that breath the basti became Ayodhya, Persepolis, Lahore Fort, Karbala, Mohenjo-daro rising from mud.

A cracked bowl flashed like a shield. A torn dupatta became a battle standard. The lane, with its sewage and smoke and frying oil, became the royal road on which heroes return after exile. The Leader’s footsteps seemed to leave not prints but promises. Even the dust rose around him ceremonially, gilding his ankles, blessing the hems of those who pressed near.

“Look,” whispered a grandmother to the child at her side. “Remember this. One day you will say you saw him come here.”

The child looked.

He saw only a tall man surrounded by other men, a white sleeve, a tired smile, a hand touching heads as though counting them. But later—because memory is the first poet of poverty—he would remember light breaking over the tin roofs, remember the lane swelling like a river, remember the Leader as vast as any king painted on a truck’s rear panel: eyes forward, sword invisible, riding not a horse but the desperate hope of those who had waited all their lives for someone to enter the place everyone else passed by.

And when the convoy left, the basti did not immediately return to itself.

For a while, people stood in the disturbed dust, blinking. They examined the ground where he had walked. They repeated his words, altering them slightly each time, polishing them into prophecy. Someone claimed he had promised houses. Someone else said jobs. Another said water. A fourth said only, “He saw us.”

That was enough for the miracle to survive the afternoon.

By evening the drains stank again. The electricity failed. The kite made from the torn poster lifted once more above the roofs, trembling against a bruised sky. But now, whenever it dipped, the children shouted as if calling back an army:

“He came here! He came here!”

And in the dark, the basti held the story close—not as fact, not yet as betrayal, but as ember.

A king had entered the slum.

For one impossible hour, the poor had watched the world kneel low enough to meet their eyes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic scene about Bhutto in Karachi after coming to power, including a half-insane impoverished woman, a Ka’ba metaphor, and the idea that no king had ever shown such mercy.
counterfactuals.output:
Karachi had not yet learned how to sleep under its new banners.

All night the city breathed in salt and kerosene, in the cries of hawkers folding up their carts, in the far-off thunder of buses painted like wedding drums. Above the harbor, gulls wheeled like scraps of torn paper, and the lights of ships trembled on the black water as if the sea itself were reading news from another country.

Then Bhutto came.

He came through streets feverish with dust and roses, through Lyari and Saddar and the old quarters where balconies leaned close together like gossiping women. Men climbed poles to see him. Boys ran beside the motorcade until their bare heels struck sparks from the road. Women lifted children toward the air, as though power were a monsoon and one might catch it in a baby’s open hands.

On every wall his name bloomed:  
**Bhutto.**  
On every tongue it became a promise, a wager, a prayer.

And in the crush near the roadside stood a half-insane impoverished woman, her hair loose beneath a torn dupatta, her wrists rattling with bangles of tin. She had slept under stairways and in the shade of shuttered shops; she had quarreled with invisible creditors; she had fed pigeons crumbs she could not spare. Yet when the crowd surged and the car slowed, she lifted both arms and laughed with a voice cracked by hunger.

“Look,” she cried, “the door has opened!”

To her, the city had become a Ka’ba of longing, and the people circled it in their grief, again and again, seeking a glimpse of the black stone of mercy. At its center was not a cube of ancient stone, but a man in a dark suit, raising his hand from an open car, his face lit by flashbulbs and expectation.

Someone shouted that bread would come.

Someone shouted that land would come.

Someone shouted that justice, long buried under files and boots and the cold signatures of the powerful, would rise from its grave.

The woman pressed forward until the police recoiled from her madness or her sanctity. She flung a garland not of flowers but of rags knotted together, and it fell short, crushed beneath a thousand feet. Still she laughed. Still she wept. Still she blessed him in a language made of broken Urdu, street dust, and the old ache of the poor.

And the rumor moved through the multitude like wind through date palms:

No king had ever shown such mercy.

No king had ever bent his ear so low.

No king had ever allowed the barefoot to believe, even for an afternoon in Karachi’s burning light, that the palace gates might open inward, and that history itself might step down from its marble chair to walk among them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Rushdie-like magical realist passage connecting Bhutto’s 1972 Karachi procession with the Shahnamah, Alexander in a red robe, and the emotional spectacle of a leader embracing poverty.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Salman Rushdie’s exact style, but here’s an original magical-realist passage with a similarly exuberant, historical, and myth-saturated energy:

In Karachi in 1972, the procession moved like a newly awakened sea, each citizen a wave with a throat, each throat carrying the salt of injury and hope. Banners swelled above the road; slogans rose and broke against balconies; children climbed lampposts as if the city had grown metal trees overnight. And at the center of this human tide came the leader, smiling with the practiced sorrow of kings and the theatrical tenderness of saints, opening his arms to the poor as though poverty were not a wound but a long-lost relative returned from exile.

That day, people said, the pavement softened under his feet. The dust became script. From the gutter-water and the heat-haze stepped figures older than the republic: Rustam with his mace shadowing the crowd, Sohrab pale with unfinished questions, kings of the *Shahnamah* leaning down from invisible balconies to inspect this modern claimant to destiny. Even Alexander appeared, not as the cold marble conqueror of schoolbooks, but wrapped in a red robe bright as a fresh slogan, red as sacrifice, red as the lining of history when it is turned inside out. He stood at the edge of the procession, smiling ambiguously, as if he recognized in this city’s fever the old appetite of empire dressed now in the language of the people.

The leader stepped from his car and embraced a laborer whose shirt was torn at the shoulder. Cameras flashed; women wept; men shouted until their voices became birds. In that instant, poverty itself seemed to acquire a body—thin, barefoot, astonished—and was folded against the immaculate chest of power. The crowd gasped at the miracle: not that hunger had ended, not that sorrow had been dismissed, but that suffering had been seen, held up, kissed before witnesses.

Above them the afternoon sun burned like a royal seal. Karachi trembled between epic and election, between ancient throne-room and asphalt road. And somewhere in the noise, a question, small as a grain of sand, entered the city’s mouth: when a king embraces the poor, does he become one of them, or do they become part of his crown?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
